facts.fact: Indian languages fall into four families: Indo-Aryan, Dravidian, Sino-Tibetan and Austric.
Indo-Aryan languages are spoken by about 74% of Indians.
Tamil is the oldest and Telugu the largest Dravidian language.
Brahmi, written left to right, is the parent of most Indian scripts.
Kharosthi was written right to left.
Tamil became the first classical language in 2004.
Telugu and Kannada became classical languages in 2008.
Marathi, Pali, Prakrit, Assamese and Bengali became classical in 2024.
The Tolkappiyam is the oldest Tamil grammar.
The Tirukkural of Thiruvalluvar is a work on ethics.
Silappadikaram and Manimekalai are the twin Tamil epics.
The Akbarnama was written by Abul Fazl.
Tarikh-i-Firuz Shahi was written by Zia-ud-din Barani.
Iqbal wrote 'Saare Jahan Se Achcha'.
The Kavitrayam — Nannaya, Tikkana, Errana — rendered the Telugu Mahabharata.
Krishnadevaraya wrote Amuktamalyada.
Allasani Peddana wrote Manucharitra.
There are six orthodox (Astika) schools that accept the Vedas.
Charvaka is not an orthodox school.
Samkhya (Kapila) is the oldest school.
Advaita was taught by Shankaracharya.
Ajivika (Makkhali Gosala) taught determinism.
Ajnana (Sanjaya Belatthiputta) taught scepticism.
Classical dance rests on Bharata Muni's Natya Shastra.
Tandava is the vigorous and Lasya the graceful aspect of dance.
The Sangeet Natak Akademi recognises eight classical dances.
Kuchipudi is the classical dance of Andhra Pradesh.
Sattriya of Assam was introduced by Sankardev.
Odissi is called 'mobile sculpture'.
Mohiniyattam of Kerala is a Lasya solo dance.
Kathakali is the Kerala dance-drama.
Siddhendra Yogi shaped Kuchipudi.
The Carnatic Trinity is Tyagaraja, Muthuswami Dikshitar and Shyama Shastri.
M.S. Subbulakshmi was the first musician awarded the Bharat Ratna.
Tholu Bommalata is the leather shadow puppetry of Andhra Pradesh.
Yakshagana is the folk theatre of Karnataka.
Tamasha is the folk theatre of Maharashtra.
Kathputli is the string puppetry of Rajasthan.
Aryabhata gave place value, zero and the value of π.
Brahmagupta gave rules for zero and negative numbers.
Varahamihira wrote the Brihat Samhita.
Sushruta pioneered surgery, including rhinoplasty.
Atukuri Molla wrote a Telugu Ramayana.
Middle Indo-Aryan (600 BCE–1000 CE) comprises Prakrit, Pali and Apabhramsha.
Apabhramsha was the transitional stage between Middle and Modern Indo-Aryan.
Pali, the language of Magadha, carries the Buddhist Tripitaka.
Prakrit is the language of the Jain Agamas.
Brahui, Malto and Kurukh are Northern Dravidian languages.
Gondi, Kui and Gadaba are (South-)Central Dravidian languages.
Manipuri (Meitei), Bhutia, Ladakhi and Sherpa are Tibeto-Burman languages.
Ahom, a Tai (Siamese-Chinese) language, is now extinct.
Kannada's classical works include the Kavirajamarga and Pampa Bharata.
The Sarala Mahabharata is a landmark of classical Odia.
The Dnyaneshwari is a landmark of classical Marathi.
The Prakrit anthology Gaha Sattasai is ascribed to the Satavahana king Hala.
The Buranjis are the chronicles of classical Assamese.
Classical status brings international awards for scholars, centres of excellence and university chairs.
The Eighth Schedule lists 22 languages; the 92nd Amendment (2003) added Bodo, Dogri, Maithili and Santhali.
The Gupta script evolved into Nagari and Bengali.
Tamil-Brahmi (from the 3rd c. BCE) appears in cave inscriptions and on pottery.
Grantha was used to write Sanskrit in the Tamil country.
Sharada was the script of Kashmir.
Siddham influenced the Tibetan and Japanese scripts.
The Aitareya Brahmana belongs to the Rigveda.
The Shatapatha Brahmana explains the Yajurveda.
The Brihadaranyaka (Yajnavalkya) is the oldest Upanishad.
'Satyameva Jayate' comes from the Mundaka Upanishad.
Kiratarjuniya was written by Bharavi.
Shishupala Vadha was written by Magha.
Dashakumaracharita was written by Dandin.
Uttararamacharita was written by Bhavabhuti.
Buddhacharita was written by Ashvaghosha.
Mudrarakshasa was written by Vishakhadatta.
Ratnavali and Nagananda were written by Harsha.
The Ashtadhyayi (Sanskrit grammar) was written by Panini.
The Amarakosha (lexicon) was compiled by Amarasimha.
Kadambari was written by Banabhatta.
The Panchatantra was written by Vishnu Sharma.
The Hitopadesha was compiled by Narayana.
Meghaduta, Raghuvamsa, Kumarasambhavam and Ritusamhara are by Kalidasa.
Tulsidas wrote the Ramcharitmanas in Awadhi (1574).
Kambar wrote the Tamil Ramayana (12th c.).
Narayaneeyam was written by Melpathur Narayana Bhattathiri.
Akananuru is the Sangam anthology of love poems; Purananuru of war and heroism.
Babur wrote his memoirs, the Tuzuk-i-Baburi (Baburnama), in Turkish.
Malik Muhammad Jayasi wrote Padmavat (c. 1540) in Awadhi.
Tabaqat-i-Nasiri was written by Minhaj-us-Siraj.
Futuh-us-Salatin was written by Isami.
Khazain-ul-Futuh, an account of Alauddin Khalji's conquests, is by Amir Khusrau.
Kitab-ul-Hind (in Arabic) was written by Al-Biruni.
The Rihla (travelogue) was written by Ibn Battuta.
Fawaid-ul-Fuad, conversations of Nizamuddin Auliya, was compiled by Amir Hasan Sijzi.
Dara Shikoh translated the Upanishads into Persian as Sirr-i-Akbar.
The Zafarnama was a Persian letter of Guru Gobind Singh to Aurangzeb.
The Chachnama, a history of the conquest of Sindh, was written by Ali Kufi.
Tagore won the Nobel Prize for Literature in 1913 for Gitanjali.
Bankim Chandra's Anandamath (1882) contains 'Vande Mataram'.
Bankim's Rajmohan's Wife (1864) was the first Indian novel in English.
Premchand's Godaan (1936) is a novel of peasant life.
Mulk Raj Anand's Untouchable (1935) attacked caste discrimination.
Raja Rao's Kanthapura (1938) has Gandhian themes.
U.R. Ananthamurthy's Kannada novel Samskara (1965) critiques caste.
Bhisham Sahni's Tamas is a Partition novel.
Jaishankar Prasad wrote the Hindi epic Kamayani.
Booker winners: Midnight's Children (Rushdie, 1981), The God of Small Things (Roy, 1997), The Inheritance of Loss (Desai, 2006), The White Tiger (Adiga, 2008).
Aravind Adiga's The White Tiger won the Booker Prize in 2008.
'Darshana', the Indian word for philosophy, means intuitive vision.
The Sarva Darshana Samgraha, a digest of Indian systems, was written by Madhavacharya (Vidyaranya).
The three debts (rinas) are to the teacher (Guru), ancestors (Pitru) and gods (Deva).
The four purusharthas are Dharma, Artha, Kama and Moksha.
Samkhya's theory of causation, Satkaryavada, holds that the effect pre-exists in the cause.
Nyaya accepts four pramanas: perception, inference, comparison (upamana) and testimony.
Mimamsa adds postulation (arthapatti) and non-perception (anupalabdhi) to reach five or six pramanas.
Kumarila Bhatta and Prabhakara were the great commentators of Mimamsa.
The eight limbs of Patanjali's yoga run from yama and niyama to dhyana and samadhi.
Vaisheshika holds the universe is made of five dravyas — earth, water, fire, air and ether — built of atoms (anu).
Charvaka accepts only perception and four elements, rejecting rebirth, soul and God.
Buddhism teaches anatta — there is no permanent self.
The Jain doctrine Syadvada holds every statement true only from a particular viewpoint.
Digambara monks wear no clothes; Svetambaras wear white.
Nimbarka taught Dvaitadvaita (dualistic non-dualism).
Vallabhacharya taught Shuddhadvaita (pure non-dualism).
Chaitanya taught Achintya Bhedabheda.
Nandikeshvara's Abhinaya Darpana describes nritta, nritya and natya.
Bibhatsa is the rasa of disgust; Adbhuta that of wonder.
Bhayanaka is the rasa of fear (horror).
Rukmini Devi Arundale took Bharatanatyam from temple to stage and founded Kalakshetra (1936).
T. Balasaraswati was a great traditional Bharatanatyam dancer.
Lady Leela Sokhey (Menaka) revived the classical style of Kathak.
The Lucknow gharana of Kathak grew at the court of Nawab Wajid Ali Shah.
Janaki Prasad founded the Banaras gharana of Kathak.
Pandit Birju Maharaj was the leading Kathak dancer of the Lucknow gharana.
Sitara Devi was hailed as the 'Empress' of Kathak.
The poet Vallathol Narayana Menon revived Kathakali and Mohiniyattam through the Kerala Kalamandalam (1930).
Kathakali and Mohiniyattam songs are in Manipravalam (Malayalam–Sanskrit).
Kathakali is accompanied by the chenda and maddalam drums.
Kalamandalam Gopi is a famous Kathakali artist.
Odissi descends from the temple dance of the Maharis; its earliest evidence is at Udayagiri–Khandagiri.
The tribhanga (three-bend) posture is characteristic of Odissi.
Kelucharan Mohapatra led the 20th-century revival of Odissi.
Sanjukta Panigrahi was a celebrated Odissi dancer.
Pung Cholom is the Manipuri drum dance.
Guru Bipin Singh was the great guru of Manipuri dance.
Kalamandalam Kalyanikutty Amma is the 'Mother of Mohiniyattam'.
Mohiniyattam has about forty basic movements called atavukal.
Abul Hasan Tana Shah of Golconda granted Kuchipudi village to its Bhagavathalu (1678).
In Kuchipudi, tarakas are chanted rhythmic syllables and angikams the body expressions.
Sattriya grew out of the Ankia Naat dance-dramas of the Assamese sattras.
The Sangeet Natak Akademi recognised Sattriya as classical in 2000.
Sattriya has a masculine style (Paurashik Bhangi) and a feminine style (Stri Bhangi).
Mayurbhanj Chhau (Odisha) is danced without masks; Purulia (WB) and Seraikella (Jharkhand) Chhau use masks.
Chhau was inscribed on UNESCO's Intangible Heritage list in 2010.
Dhimsa is a tribal dance of Andhra Pradesh (Araku–Visakhapatnam agency).
Veeranatyam, the 'dance of the brave' in honour of Shiva, is from Andhra Pradesh.
Kolattam is the stick dance of Andhra Pradesh.
Saang of Haryana was originated by Kishan Lal Bhaat (1750).
Dhamal is danced by Ahir men of Haryana at harvest.
Nati is the circle dance of Himachal Pradesh.
Karam is danced at the Karam festival in Jharkhand.
Dollu Kunitha is the drum dance of Karnataka.
Huli Vesha (tiger dance) is performed in coastal Karnataka at Dasara.
Theyyam is the ritual dance of Kerala's Malabar region.
Ottamthullal is a solo satirical Kerala form (Kunchan Nambiar).
The Matki dance with pots belongs to Bundelkhand / Madhya Pradesh.
Lavani is the folk dance-song of Maharashtra.
The Koli dance is the fisherfolk dance of coastal Maharashtra.
Thang Ta is the martial dance of Manipur.
Gotipua of Odisha is danced by young boys dressed as girls.
Dalkhai is a women's dance of western Odisha.
Gidda is the women's folk dance of Punjab.
Kalbeliya, the serpentine dance of Rajasthan, is on UNESCO's ICH list (2010).
Bhavai of Rajasthan is danced balancing pots on the head.
Kachchhi Ghodi of Rajasthan uses dummy horses.
Karagattam of Tamil Nadu honours Mariamman with pots on the head.
Mayil Attam is the peacock dance of Tamil Nadu.
Garba of Gujarat was inscribed on UNESCO's ICH list in 2023.
Bihu is the festival dance of Assam.
The Gwalior gharana, the oldest khayal gharana, traces to Nathan Peerbaksh.
Bade Ghulam Ali Khan was the star of the Patiala gharana.
The Kirana gharana of Abdul Karim Khan produced Bhimsen Joshi and Gangubai Hangal.
Pandit Jasraj belonged to the Mewati gharana.
The Jaipur-Atrauli gharana of Alladiya Khan includes Kishori Amonkar and Mallikarjun Mansur.
Ustad Faiyaz Khan was the great singer of the Agra gharana.
Ustad Rashid Khan belonged to the Rampur-Sahaswan gharana.
Purandara Dasa is called the 'Pitamaha' (father) of Carnatic music.
Varnam and kriti are the two key composition forms of Carnatic music.
The Tanjore Quartet (Chinnayya, Ponnayya, Sivanandam, Vadivelu) systematised Bharatanatyam music.
M.S. Subbulakshmi, D.K. Pattammal and M.L. Vasanthakumari are the female trinity of Carnatic music.
Begum Akhtar was the 'Mallika-e-Ghazal'.
Amir Khusrau, disciple of Nizamuddin Auliya, is linked with qawwali and the sitar.
The Gundecha Brothers sang dhrupad in the Dagar vani.
The Natya Shastra classes instruments as tata (string), sushira (wind), avanaddha (drum) and ghana (solid).
Baul is the mystic song of Bengal, sung to the ektara.
Bhatiali is the boatmen's song of Bengal.
Powada is Maharashtra's heroic ballad (e.g. on Shivaji).
Kajri is sung by women of UP in the rainy season.
Mando is the Goan song blending Indian and Western music.
Pandavani, Chhattisgarh's Mahabharata narration, was made famous by Teejan Bai.
Villu Pattu is the bow song of Tamil Nadu.
Maand of Rajasthan glorifies the Rajput rulers.
The Sitabenga and Jogimara caves (Chhattisgarh) are counted among the oldest amphitheatres.
Lokadharmi plays are realistic; natyadharmi plays are stylised.
Koodiyattam of Kerala, the oldest living Sanskrit theatre, was proclaimed by UNESCO in 2001.
Ramman of Uttarakhand (Garhwal) is UNESCO-listed (2009).
Mudiyettu of Kerala enacts Kali's battle with Darika (UNESCO 2010).
Jatra is the open-air folk theatre of Bengal.
Bhavai is the folk theatre of Gujarat.
Nautanki is the folk theatre of Uttar Pradesh.
Swang is the folk theatre of Haryana.
Maach is the folk theatre of Madhya Pradesh.
Bhand Pather is the satirical theatre of Kashmir.
Therukoothu is the street theatre of Tamil Nadu.
Krishnattam of Kerala depicts the life of Krishna.
Dashavatar is the Konkan–Goa theatre of the ten avatars.
Oja-Pali is a narrative chorus form of Assam.
Pagati Veshalu is the street-guise folk theatre of Andhra Pradesh.
The Sangeet Natak Akademi was set up in 1952 and the National School of Drama in 1959.
Bommalattam (TN) has the largest and heaviest puppets, combining rod and string.
Gombeyatta of Karnataka is a string puppetry styled on Yakshagana.
Kundhei is the string puppetry of Odisha.
Togalu Gombeyatta is the shadow puppetry of Karnataka.
Ravanachhaya of Odisha uses deer-skin shadow puppets.
Putul Nach is the rod puppetry of Bengal.
Yampuri is the jointless rod puppetry of Bihar.
Pavakoothu is the glove puppetry of Kerala.
Kalasutri Bahulya is the string puppetry of Maharashtra.
Meher Contractor of the Darpana Academy introduced modern puppetry to India.
Bandhani (bandhej) tie-and-dye belongs to Rajasthan and Gujarat.
Chikankari white-thread embroidery is from Lucknow.
Kantha running-stitch embroidery is from West Bengal.
Phulkari ('making flowers') embroidery is from Punjab.
Pipli appliqué work comes from Pipli village, Odisha.
Patola double-ikat silk is from Gujarat (Patan).
Toda red-and-black embroidery is from the Nilgiris.
Chanderi silk-cotton weaving is from Madhya Pradesh.
Bhagalpur (Bihar) is famed for tussar silk.
Firozabad (UP) is the glass-bangle town.
The Bankura terracotta horse comes from West Bengal.
Bidriware (silver inlay on blackened alloy) comes from Bidar, Karnataka.
Dokra is lost-wax brass casting of Odisha, Bengal and Chhattisgarh.
Pembarthi sheet-metal work comes from Telangana.
Marori work (etched metal filled with resin) is from Rajasthan.
Kolhapuri chappals are from Maharashtra.
Manoti art (decorated camel skin) is from Bikaner.
Khatamband ceilings are Kashmiri woodwork.
Channapatna (Karnataka) is the 'Toy Town of India'.
Pith (sholapith) dolls are an Assamese craft.
Makrana (Rajasthan) supplied the white marble of the Taj Mahal.
Mandana floor art belongs to Rajasthan and MP.
In Andhra Pradesh the kolam floor design is called muggulu.
Aryabhata wrote the Aryabhatiya (499 CE).
Brahmagupta wrote the Brahmasphutasiddhanta (628 CE).
Bhaskara II wrote the Lilavati, part of his Siddhanta Shiromani.
Baudhayana's Sulbasutra states the theorem later called Pythagoras'.
Pingala's Chandahshastra describes a binary-like system of metres.
Nagarjuna's Rasaratnakara describes metal purification and zinc distillation.
Vagbhata wrote the Ashtanga Hridaya (Ayurveda).
Madhava of Sangamagrama founded the Kerala school of astronomy and infinite series.
Charaka is traditionally the court physician of Kanishka.
Nalanda was founded by the Gupta king Kumaragupta I (5th c.).
Vikramashila was founded by the Pala king Dharmapala.
Odantapuri was founded by the Pala king Gopala.
Valabhi (Gujarat) flourished under the Maitrakas.
Sawai Jai Singh II built five Jantar Mantar observatories — Delhi, Jaipur, Ujjain, Varanasi and Mathura.
